title: Ezekiel 38:17–23
context: Ezekiel 38:17–23 closes the first Gog oracle with the LORD’s words. He asks, “Are you he of whom I spoke in old time by my servants the prophets of Israel”? (38:17). Which earlier prophets are meant is debated; readers point to oracles of a foe from the north such as Jeremiah 6:22, or to broader prophecies of the nations gathered against Zion, and the question form leaves the matter open. The LORD then describes his judgment on Gog in the language of a great shaking of creation (38:19–20; compare Haggai 2:6), confusion in which “Every man’s sword will be against his brother” (38:21; compare Judges 7:22; Haggai 2:22), and pestilence, torrential rain, hail, fire, and sulfur (38:22; compare Genesis 19:24). This is the language of divine judgment and theophany, and it is best read with sobriety rather than as a detailed forecast of physical events. The purpose is stated plainly: “I will magnify myself and sanctify myself, and I will make myself known in the eyes of many nations.” (38:23). Revelation 20:8–9 names “Gog and Magog” and pictures fire from heaven consuming the nations that surround the camp of the saints. The two passages differ in setting and detail: Ezekiel places Gog after Israel’s restoration to the land, while Revelation places Gog and Magog after the thousand years and describes them as nations from the four corners of the earth. Interpreters relate the two in different ways, and premillennial, amillennial, and postmillennial readers are found in both traditions.

verses.text: “ ‘The Lord GOD says: “Are you he of whom I spoke in old time by my servants the prophets of Israel, who prophesied in those days for years that I would bring you against them?
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD asks, “Are you he of whom I spoke in old time by my servants the prophets of Israel”? Arminian readers note that the identity of these prophets is debated, and they point to oracles of a foe from the north, such as Jeremiah 6:22, while holding the question open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the reference open, noting that no earlier prophet names Gog. They observe that the question may point to a broad prophetic theme of the nations gathered against Zion, and both traditions read the verse as linking Ezekiel’s oracle to earlier prophecy.

verses.text: It will happen in that day, when Gog comes against the land of Israel,” says the Lord GOD, “that my wrath will come up into my nostrils.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says that when Gog comes against the land of Israel, his wrath will come up into his nostrils. Arminian readers note the vivid anthropomorphic image of God’s anger, and they see it as expressing God’s response to an attack on the people he has restored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same image and read it as God’s righteous anger against the enemy of his people. They observe that the language is figurative, describing God in human terms, and both traditions read the verse as shared ground on God’s defense of his people.

verses.text: For in my jealousy and in the fire of my wrath I have spoken. Surely in that day there will be a great shaking in the land of Israel,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that in his jealousy and the fire of his wrath there will be a great shaking in the land of Israel. Arminian readers note the echo of Haggai 2:6, named without harmonizing, and they see the shaking as the language of God’s overwhelming intervention in judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and read the shaking as the language of theophany, God’s appearing in power. They observe that the image should be read soberly as poetic description rather than as a detailed forecast, a point both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: so that the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, the animals of the field, all creeping things who creep on the earth, and all the men who are on the surface of the earth will shake at my presence. Then the mountains will be thrown down, the steep places will fall, and every wall will fall to the ground.
verses.arminianNotes: The fish, birds, animals, creeping things, and all people will shake at God’s presence, and mountains and walls will fall. Arminian readers note that the whole creation is affected, and they see the scene as showing that no part of the world is untouched when God acts in judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same scope and read it as the language of cosmic upheaval at God’s appearing. They observe that similar imagery appears elsewhere in the prophets, and both traditions read the verse with sobriety as describing God’s majesty rather than offering a physical chronology.

verses.text: I will call for a sword against him to all my mountains,” says the Lord GOD. “Every man’s sword will be against his brother.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will call for a sword against Gog, and “Every man’s sword will be against his brother.” Arminian readers note the echo of Judges 7:22, “the LORD set every man’s sword against his fellow”, and they see the enemy defeated by its own confusion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and compare Haggai 2:22, named without harmonizing. They read the verse as showing that God defeats the enemy without his people needing to fight, a point both traditions treat as shared ground on God’s deliverance.

verses.text: I will enter into judgment with him with pestilence and with blood. I will rain on him, on his hordes, and on the many peoples who are with him, torrential rains with great hailstones, fire, and sulfur.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will enter into judgment with Gog with pestilence, blood, torrential rain, hail, fire, and sulfur. Arminian readers note the echo of Genesis 19:24, “sulfur and fire from the LORD out of the sky”, and they read the imagery soberly as the language of divine judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and read the list as a gathering of images of God’s judgment from earlier Scripture. They observe that the images should be read with sobriety, and both traditions treat the verse as shared ground on the certainty of God’s victory over evil.

verses.text: I will magnify myself and sanctify myself, and I will make myself known in the eyes of many nations. Then they will know that I am the LORD.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I will magnify myself and sanctify myself, and I will make myself known in the eyes of many nations. Then they will know that I am the LORD.” Arminian readers note that the goal of the judgment is the nations’ knowledge of God, and they see a purpose that reaches all peoples.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same goal and read it as God’s display of his glory and holiness. They observe that Revelation 20:8–9 takes up the names Gog and Magog in its own setting, with differences in detail, and both traditions include readers who relate the passages in different ways.
